newsitem.title: USA: NYC wants new bankers to deal fairly in all areas.
newsitem.headline: NYC wants new bankers to deal fairly in all areas.

text.p: New York City, which started picking bankers for its new borrowing authority, for the first time took steps to ensure both the firms and their top managers have good track records in all their dealings with the city.

"If we believe they have taken unreasonable or harsh positions and then they come around and want business from us, it might be a factor in determining whether to give them the business," said an official with the city law department, who declined to be named.

He was explaining a new provision New York City included in a request for underwriters' recommendations on selling the New York City Transitional Financing Authority's new bonds. The authority, created earlier this year to help the city sidestep its debt cap, plans to start selling bonds by late August or early September.
In fiscal 1998, New York City expects to issue about $2.774 billion of general obligation and bonds sold by the new authority, a sum that climbs to $2.820 billion in fiscal 2001.

The city, which expects to pick the new authority's bankers in May or June, took the unusual step of saying it might reshuffle the present teams for its general obligation bond and revenue bonds sold by the Municipal Water Finance Authority.

There are only about eight to 10 qualified investment bankers that are big enough and sophisticated enough to run the city's debt sales, which usually run at least $500 million, as foreign firms are not eligible, city officials said. The New York City budget director, Joe Lhota, has said he felt that banks should not hold the top and most profitable spot on more than one syndicate, according to reports.

Last summer, the city picked Merrill Lynch , Prudential Securities, Bear Stearns Cos, Lehman Brothers and Smith Barney for the rotating position of book-runner on the general obligation bond syndicate. But J.P. Morgan Securities and long-time senior manager, Goldman Sachs & Co, were shifted to the team that sells the water authority's bonds. PaineWebber also was selected for that team.

New York City said that firms would be chosen for the new top slots based on the quality of their investment banking and marketing support and their history in solving past and ongoing disputes with the city as well as for their employees' compliance in paying their taxes.

The new tax requirement covers cases like PaineWebber's which early this year won a $7.2 million case before the Tax Appeals Tribunal because the city failed to serve notice properly. The city has appealed the decision, and neither its officials nor a PaineWebber spokesman would comment about the matter. And city officials stressed that the new rule was written broadly enough to cover a wide range of disputes firms might have with New York City, not just tax battles.

The city's decision to explicitly require that top brokerage houses employees pay their taxes was tied to an income tax case in which a senior official at one financial firm plead guility to a misdemeanor after being turned in for claiming he lived outside New York City. "There really was no defense," a city official said.

More emphasis also was put on marketing services provided by underwriters. "The specific question about marketing set this apart from other Requests for Proposals that we put out," said an official said, who also declined to be named.

For the first time since January, 1994, New York City included questions on compensation, asking bankers if they should be paid more for the authority's first sale--which will set the tone for future offerings--than for subsequent ones.

Underwriters, who specifically were asked not to call rating agencies in an effort to force the bankers to be more creative and to spare rating analysts from a deluge of calls, were asked to recommend strategies to wall off the authority's new debt from the city's general obligations.
Proposals for various kinds of debt structures, including variable rate and short-term debt, also were sought.
